title: Come and see (John 1:29–39)
hook: John points, two disciples follow, and Jesus asks what seek you

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line that made a church kneel: eskenosen, the Word made flesh. Your line was and dwelt among us. Where did you notice the place you live? Day four hundred ninety-four.

Bethania, beyond the Jordan. John is baptizing there when he sees a man walking toward him, and he points. What he says next is a line the priest repeats at Mass just before Communion, lifting the host: behold the Lamb of God. It didn't come from a council or a liturgist. It came from a riverbank. Today we stand at that river and hear it said, and watch what two people do the moment they hear it.
screen: `BETHANIA, BEYOND THE JORDAN.` → `A MAN WALKING TOWARD HIM.` → `A LINE NOW SAID AT MASS.`

segments.voice: John the Baptist sees Jesus coming and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." Lamb of God is today's word, and it's a strange thing to call a man. Readers hear in it the Passover lamb, whose blood marked the doors in Egypt, the lambs offered every day in the temple, and Isaiah's servant, led as a sheep to the slaughter. John packs all of that into one name. The next day he says it again, and this time two of his own disciples hear him, and they simply leave him and follow Jesus. Jesus turns around, sees them trailing behind, and asks the first words he speaks in this Gospel: "What seek you?" Not who are you, not what do you believe. What are you looking for? They answer with a question of their own: Rabbi, where do you live? And he says: "Come and see." No sermon. No test. Just an invitation to come along and look. They came, and saw where he abode, and stayed with him that day; John even remembers the hour, about the tenth hour, late in the afternoon. One of the two, the Gospel says, was Andrew. The other is never named. Some readers have thought it was the writer himself, remembering the afternoon his life turned. The Church has kept John's pointing finger at the center of the Mass. The Lamb of God is sung while the bread is broken. And then the priest lifts the host, points as John pointed, and says: behold.
screen: `JOHN POINTS: BEHOLD THE LAMB.` · `PASSOVER, TEMPLE, ISAIAH.` · `WHAT SEEK YOU?` · `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer what are you seeking. Settle, and breathe. Imagine someone turning around on a path and asking you, kindly and directly: what are you looking for? Don't give the answer you think you should give. Let the real one come up. Maybe peace. Maybe a person. Maybe just rest. Maybe you don't know, and that's an answer too. Stay with it. If you pray, you can tell God plainly what you're seeking. If you don't, just let yourself hear your own answer. The bell holds the time.
Agnus Dei. The Latin for Lamb of God, John the Baptist's name for Jesus at the Jordan, sung again at every Mass before Communion. Today's word.
Your line: what seek you. Today, when you want something, pause and ask yourself honestly what you're really seeking. Day four hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: At every Mass the Lamb of God (Agnus Dei) is sung or said while the priest breaks the host, and just before Communion he holds it up and repeats John the Baptist's words, behold the Lamb of God.

myth: the line behold the Lamb of God was written for the Mass
it's John the Baptist's, at the Jordan (John 1:29). the Mass borrows it.
Jesus's first words in John's Gospel are a question
the Gospel names both disciples who followed
it names Andrew; the other is unnamed, and some readers have thought it was the writer himself.

fork.setup: you're one of John the Baptist's disciples. he points at a man walking by and says: behold the Lamb of God. what do you do?
options: follow the man down the road.
fork.reveal: two of them simply follow. Jesus turns, asks what seek you, and says come and see. they stay with him that day.

original.note: Greek: lamb of God (John 1:29); in Latin, Agnus Dei, the words sung at Mass.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lamb of God means Jesus was gentle.
what it means: John is calling Jesus the one whose sacrifice takes away the sin of the world.
what a scholar hears: amnos tou theou gathers the Passover lamb, the daily temple lambs and Isaiah 53's lamb led to slaughter into one title.

sources.quoted: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world.

notes: The Mass wording ('behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world') is described from the current Missal and not quoted as a source; the ICEL translation is copyrighted. Confirm the paraphrase is acceptable.
Tenth hour as about four in the afternoon (counting from sunrise): the common reading. Confirm.
Unnamed disciple as the beloved disciple/the writer: stated as many readers' view since early times. Confirm.
'What seek you?' as Jesus's first words in John: confirm.
Verse numbering: Douay John 1:38–39 match the quotations used. Confirm.

Editor review (483-500 pass): John's Gospel has no camel hair and does not put John in the river (cut; now Bethania beyond the Jordan, 1:28); 'four words' was a wrong count (cut); 'every Catholic knows by heart', 'three times', 'many readers since early times' and 'four in the afternoon' softened to the text's tenth hour; hook no longer opens 'At every Mass' like day 486.
